seo.shortDescription: Searchable duty table for all 312 HTS Chapter 48 lines: newsprint, printing and copy paper, kraft paper, coated board, tissue, toilet paper, boxes, bags, notebooks, labels and paper cups. Every base rate is Free; see the Section 301, Canada Section 338 and China duties by country and the AD/CVD orders on paper products.

overview.intro:
Chapter 48 covers paper and paperboard and the things made from them: **newsprint** (4801), **printing, writing and copy paper** (4802), **kraft paper and linerboard** (4804), **fluting and recycled board** (4805), **coated paper and board** (4810, 4811), **toilet paper, tissues, towels and napkins** (4818), **boxes, cartons and bags** (4819), **notebooks and binders** (4820), **labels** (4821) and **paper cups, plates and molded pulp** (4823). Every one of its **312 tariff lines is Free** at the general rate.

So the extra duty by country decides the cost. Since **July 24, 2026** goods from 60 economies pay a **Section 301 duty of 10% or 12.5%** on every Chapter 48 line; no paper line is on its exemption list. Canadian and Mexican goods that qualify for **USMCA** are exempt, but **62 Canadian lines** (among them corrugated boxes, kraftliner, writing paper, envelopes, napkins, notebooks and paper cups) pay a **50% Section 338 duty** since August 22, 2026, even with a USMCA claim. China pays **25% (List 3) or 7.5% (List 4A) plus 12.5%**, and Brazil **37.5%**. Many paper products also carry **antidumping or countervailing duties**: thermal paper, uncoated and coated printing paper, paper plates, molded fiber tableware, shopping bags, file folders, lined paper, tissue and crepe paper and gift boxes. The U.S. imported **$19.94B** of Chapter 48 goods in 2025, a third of it from Canada.

productGroups.label: Newsprint
productGroups.blurb: Newsprint in rolls or sheets: 2 lines, Free. Almost all U.S. newsprint imports come from Canada, Free with USMCA and 10% without; newsprint is not on the Section 338 list.

productGroups.label: Uncoated printing, writing & copy paper
productGroups.blurb: Uncoated paper for writing, printing and copying, including copy paper, offset paper and paper base for thermal or photo paper: 56 lines, Free. From Canada, writing and cover paper in rolls (4802.55.10) and the mechanical-pulp grades of 4802.61–4802.69 (13 lines) pay 50% under Section 338; certain uncoated paper is under AD/CVD orders.

productGroups.label: Tissue & towel stock (parent rolls)
productGroups.blurb: Toilet, facial tissue, towel and napkin stock and cellulose wadding in large rolls or sheets: 2 lines, Free. Since September 15, 2026 not on the Canada Section 338 list.

productGroups.label: Uncoated kraft paper & paperboard (kraftliner, sack kraft)
productGroups.blurb: Uncoated kraft paper and board in rolls or sheets: kraftliner, sack kraft, wrapping paper and cup and carton stock, 30 lines, Free. Canadian unbleached kraftliner (4804.11) pays 50% under Section 338.

productGroups.label: Other uncoated paper & paperboard (fluting, testliner, recycled board)
productGroups.blurb: Corrugating medium (semichemical and recycled fluting), testliner, filter and felt paper, pressboard and tube and core board: 30 lines, Free. Not on the Section 338 lists.

productGroups.label: Vegetable parchment, greaseproof, tracing paper & glassine
productGroups.blurb: Vegetable parchment, greaseproof paper, tracing paper and glassine: 4 lines, Free. Canadian greaseproof paper (4806.20) pays 50% under Section 338.

productGroups.label: Composite (laminated) paper & paperboard
productGroups.blurb: Paper and board made by gluing flat layers together, including bitumen-laminated and cloth-reinforced paper: 4 lines, Free.

productGroups.label: Corrugated, creped & embossed paper
productGroups.blurb: Corrugated paper and board in rolls or sheets, creped kraft paper and other creped, embossed or perforated paper: 5 lines, Free. Crepe paper from China is under an antidumping order.

productGroups.label: Carbon & self-copy paper (large rolls or sheets)
productGroups.blurb: Carbon paper, self-copy (carbonless) paper and other copying or transfer paper in large rolls or sheets: 7 lines, Free.

productGroups.label: Coated paper & paperboard (clay-coated)
productGroups.blurb: Paper and board coated with kaolin or other inorganic substances: coated freesheet, light-weight coated paper, coated bleached and recycled board, 65 lines, Free. Five Canadian lines pay 50% under Section 338; sheet-fed coated paper from China and Indonesia is under AD/CVD orders.

productGroups.label: Paper coated with plastics, wax or adhesive; thermal & gift wrap
productGroups.blurb: Paper and board coated, impregnated or covered with plastics, wax, adhesive or other materials: self-adhesive label stock, poly-coated cupstock, wax paper, direct thermal paper and gift wrap, 35 lines, Free. 14 Canadian lines pay 50% under Section 338; thermal paper is under AD orders.

productGroups.label: Filter blocks, slabs & plates of paper pulp
productGroups.blurb: Filter blocks, slabs and plates of paper pulp: 1 line, Free.

productGroups.label: Cigarette paper
productGroups.blurb: Cigarette paper in booklets or tubes, in narrow rolls or in other forms: 3 lines, Free. Canadian booklets and tubes (4813.10) pay 50% under Section 338.

productGroups.label: Wallpaper & wallcoverings
productGroups.blurb: Wallpaper and similar wallcoverings and window transparencies of paper: 2 lines, Free. China pays 7.5% (List 4A) plus 12.5%; Canadian plastic-coated wallpaper (4814.20) pays 50% under Section 338.

productGroups.label: Carbon & self-copy paper (cut, boxed)
productGroups.blurb: Carbon paper, self-copy paper and other copying or transfer papers cut to size, whether or not in boxes: 2 lines, Free.

productGroups.label: Envelopes & correspondence cards
productGroups.blurb: Envelopes, letter cards, plain postcards and boxed stationery: 4 lines, Free. Canadian envelopes (4817.10) pay 50% under Section 338.

productGroups.label: Toilet paper, tissues, towels & napkins
productGroups.blurb: Household and sanitary paper cut to size: toilet paper, facial tissues, paper towels, napkins and tablecloths, paper gowns and face masks, 8 lines, Free. Canadian napkins and paper face masks pay 50% under Section 338; China pays 37.5% (20% on 4818.90).

productGroups.label: Boxes, cartons, bags & paper packaging
productGroups.blurb: Cartons, boxes and bags of paper or board: corrugated boxes, folding cartons, paper bags and sacks, fiber drums and office storage boxes, 14 lines, Free. Seven Canadian lines (corrugated boxes, small bags, other containers) pay 50% under Section 338; shopping bags and gift boxes carry AD/CVD orders.

productGroups.label: Notebooks, diaries, binders & business forms
productGroups.blurb: Registers, notebooks, diaries, memo pads, exercise books, binders, folders, business forms and albums: 12 lines, Free. Canadian notebooks, diaries and binders pay 50% under Section 338; lined paper and file folders carry AD/CVD orders.

productGroups.label: Paper labels
productGroups.blurb: Paper and paperboard labels, printed or not, including self-adhesive labels: 4 lines, Free. Canadian unprinted non-adhesive labels (4821.90.40) pay 50% under Section 338.

productGroups.label: Bobbins, spools & cores
productGroups.blurb: Bobbins, spools, cops and similar supports of paper pulp, paper or board, including textile-yarn cones: 2 lines, Free.

productGroups.label: Paper cups, plates, molded pulp & other paper articles
productGroups.blurb: Paper cups, plates, trays and bowls, molded pulp articles, filter paper, recording-chart paper, paper gaskets and other cut paper: 20 lines, Free. Eight Canadian lines pay 50% under Section 338; paper plates and molded fiber tableware carry AD/CVD orders.

workedExamples.title: $1M of copy paper from Canada
workedExamples.body: Letter-size uncoated copy paper made of chemical pulp falls in 4802.56 (sheets with one side not over 435 mm and the other not over 297 mm). The base rate is **Free** and 4802.56 is not on the Section 338 list. With a USMCA claim, U.S. note 52(g) (9903.05.93) lifts the 10% Section 301 duty on Canada, so the duty is **$0**; without the claim it is **$100,000** (9903.05.29). Uncoated paper from Brazil, Indonesia, Portugal, China and Australia is also under antidumping orders, which this table does not include.

workedExamples.title: $1M of corrugated boxes from Canada
workedExamples.body: 4819.10.00 is on the Section 338 list in U.S. note 51(b)(3), so Canadian corrugated boxes pay **50%** (9903.03.14) since August 22, 2026. Note 51(a) applies it even when USMCA is claimed: **$500,000**. Without a USMCA claim the 10% Section 301 duty is added: **$600,000**. The same boxes from Mexico are Free with USMCA.

workedExamples.title: $1M of toilet paper from China
workedExamples.body: Toilet paper is Free at base. From China it pays the 2018 Section 301 List 3 duty of **25%** (9903.88.03) plus the 2026 Section 301 duty of **12.5%** (9903.05.31): **$375,000**. From Indonesia it pays 10% (9903.05.45); from Canada or Mexico with USMCA, $0.

workedExamples.title: $1M of paper plates from Vietnam
workedExamples.body: Paper plates are Free at base and pay the 12.5% Section 301 duty on Vietnam (9903.05.84): **$125,000**. They are also inside the 2025 antidumping and countervailing duty orders on paper plates from Vietnam (90 FR 13139, 90 FR 13135), so CBP collects cash deposits at the company-specific rates in those orders on top. The tariff calculator does not include AD/CVD.

notes.chapterNotes:
**Note 1.** "Paper" includes paperboard, whatever its thickness or weight.

**Note 2.** The chapter does not cover, among others: articles of chapter 30; perfumed or cosmetic papers (chapter 33); paper impregnated with soap, detergent or polishes (3401, 3405); sensitized paper (3701–3704); paper-reinforced plastic sheeting or paper coated with plastics thicker than the paper (chapter 39), other than wallcoverings of 4814; travel goods of 4202; abrasive paper (6805); metal foil backed with paper; toys and games (chapter 95); or sanitary pads, tampons and diapers (chapter 96).

**Note 4.** "Newsprint" is uncoated paper for printing newspapers, at least 50% mechanical or chemi-mechanical wood fiber, unsized or very lightly sized, 40–65 g/m², in rolls wider than 28 cm or large sheets.

**Note 5.** Heading 4802 covers writing, printing and graphic paper made mainly from bleached or mechanical pulp that meets fiber, ash, brightness and burst tests; it excludes filter paper (including teabag paper) and felt paper.

**Note 6.** "Kraft paper" has at least 80% of its fiber from the chemical sulfate or soda process.

**Note 7.** Paper that fits two or more of headings 4801–4811 goes in the one that comes last.

**Note 8.** Headings 4803–4809 cover only rolls wider than 36 cm or sheets with one side over 36 cm and the other over 15 cm; smaller cut sizes go to 4816–4823.

**Note 9.** Heading 4814 wallpaper is paper in rolls 45–160 cm wide, decorated, textured or plastic-faced, plus borders and panel murals.

**Note 12.** Except for 4814 and 4821, paper articles printed with motifs, characters or pictures that are not merely subsidiary to their use fall in chapter 49.

**Subheading notes 1–7** define kraftliner (over 115 g/m² with a minimum Mullen burst), sack kraft paper (60–115 g/m²), semichemical and straw fluting, testliner (recycled), sulfite wrapping paper and light-weight coated paper (up to 72 g/m², mechanical-pulp base).

**Statistical note 1** defines "standard newsprint paper" (46.3–57 g/m², minimum roll and sheet sizes, ash up to 6.5%); **statistical note 2** requires paper shoe covers (4823.90.8620) to be at least 50% cellulose or paper by weight.

seo.shortDescription: What changed for paper and paperboard imports since January 2025: the IEEPA duties and their end, the Section 122 surcharge, the 2026 Section 301 and Brazil duties, the 50% Section 338 duty on 62 Canadian paper lines, China List 3, and the antidumping and countervailing duty orders on paper products, with Federal Register citations.

tariffUpdates.intro:
This page compares two editions of the tariff schedule: the **2025 Basic Edition**, in force at the start of 2025, and the current **2026 Revision 21** (in force October 9, 2026). All 312 Chapter 48 lines are **Free** in both; the base rates did not change.

The extra duties changed a lot. In 2025 non-USMCA paper from Canada and Mexico paid IEEPA duties (Canada 25%, then 35%), paper from most other countries paid the reciprocal tariff, China paid fentanyl and reciprocal duties on top of List 3, and Brazil paid another 40%. All IEEPA duties **ended on February 24, 2026**; the 10% Section 122 surcharge that replaced them expired on **July 23, 2026**.

Today: the **2026 Section 301 duties** on 60 economies (10% or 12.5% from July 24, 2026; USMCA goods exempt), **Brazil's 25% Section 301 duty** (from July 22, 2026), the **50% Section 338 duty on 62 Canadian lines** (from August 22, 2026; widened to writing and printing paper on September 15) and China's **List 3 (25%) and List 4A (7.5%)** duties. Paper products are also one of the most common targets of **antidumping and countervailing duty orders**: 12 product families are covered today, two more circumvention or injury cases are open, and a petition on corrugated pizza boxes was filed in September 2026. AD/CVD cash deposits are listed below for reference and are **not included in the tariff calculator**.

For the rate each supplier pays, see Rates by country.

changes.title: No Chapter 48 base-rate changes
changes.detail: All 312 Chapter 48 tariff lines carry the same General rate (Free) in 2026 Revision 21 as in the 2025 Basic Edition; no line was added, removed or renumbered.

changes.title: Antidumping and countervailing duty orders on paper products
changes.detail: Commerce orders in force on Chapter 48 goods, with the HTS numbers their scopes list: thermal paper from Germany, Japan, South Korea and Spain (AD, 4811.90.8030 and .9030) and lightweight thermal paper from China (AD/CVD, continued January 23, 2026); certain uncoated paper from Australia, Brazil, China, Indonesia and Portugal (AD; CVD China, Indonesia; 4802.56, .57, .62, .69); sheet-fed coated paper from China and Indonesia (AD/CVD; 4810.14–4810.92); tissue paper products and crepe paper products from China (AD); lined paper products from China and India (AD; CVD India; 4820.10.20); folding gift boxes from China (AD; 4819.20.0040, 4819.50.4060); paper shopping bags from Cambodia, China, Colombia, India, Malaysia, Portugal, Taiwan, Türkiye and Vietnam (AD; CVD China, India; 4819.30.0040, 4819.40.0040); paper file folders from China, India, Vietnam and Sri Lanka (AD) and India and Cambodia (CVD; 4820.30.0040); paper plates from China, Thailand and Vietnam (AD; CVD China, Vietnam; 4823.61.0040, 4823.69.0040, 4823.70.0020); and thermoformed molded fiber products from China and Vietnam (AD/CVD; 4823.61–4823.70, 4823.90.10). Cash-deposit rates are company-specific and are not in the tariff calculator.
changes.countries: China, Vietnam, India, Indonesia, Brazil, Portugal and others

changes.title: China Section 301 duties continue during the four-year review
changes.detail: USTR received requests to continue the 2018 China actions, so they did not terminate on their 2026 anniversaries and remain in effect pending the statutory review. The 25% List 3 and 7.5% List 4A duties on Chinese paper continue.

changes.title: AD/CVD petitions on corrugated pizza boxes from China, Malaysia and Türkiye
changes.detail: On September 9, 2026 U.S. producers and the United Steelworkers petitioned for antidumping duties on corrugated die-cut cardboard (pizza) boxes from China, Malaysia and Türkiye and a countervailing duty on Türkiye (subheading 4819.10.00). The ITC instituted its preliminary investigations on September 14; Commerce extended its initiation decision to October 19, 2026 to poll industry support. No duty applies unless orders are issued.

changes.title: Five-year reviews begin for the thermal paper and tissue paper orders
changes.detail: The ITC instituted five-year (sunset) reviews of the antidumping orders on thermal paper from Germany, Japan, South Korea and Spain and on certain tissue paper products from China. The orders stay in force while the reviews run.
changes.countries: Germany, Japan, South Korea, Spain, China

changes.title: Section 338 list widened to Canadian writing and printing paper
changes.detail: Proclamation 11065 changed the list in U.S. note 51(b)(3) (9903.03.14). It added the mechanical-pulp writing, drawing and printing grades of 4802.61.10, .20, .60, 4802.62.10, .20, .30, .61 and 4802.69.10, .20, .30 (12 lines) and removed tissue stock 4803.00.40 and paper articles of 4818.90 other than face masks (4818.90.0080). Proclamation 11064 left the six Chapter 48 provisions of the alcoholic-beverages list (note 51(b)(1)) unchanged.

changes.title: Section 338: 50% on Canadian kraftliner, boxes, envelopes, napkins and more
changes.detail: Proclamations 11046 (alcoholic beverages) and 11048 (motor vehicles), signed July 20, 2026, imposed a 50% duty on listed products of Canada in response to Canada's treatment of U.S. alcoholic beverages and autos. In Chapter 48 it reached 52 lines: 11 under 9903.03.12 (kraftliner, greaseproof paper, certain coated, thermal and gift wrap paper) and 41 under 9903.03.14 (writing paper in rolls, coated board, cigarette paper booklets, wallpaper, envelopes, napkins, tissue stock, corrugated boxes, bags, containers, notebooks, binders, labels, paper cups and molded pulp). Proclamation 11056 moved the start from August 19 to August 22, 2026. The duty applies even when USMCA is claimed.

changes.title: Circumvention inquiry: tissue paper finished in Vietnam
changes.detail: Commerce opened a country-wide inquiry into whether tissue paper products completed in Vietnam from Chinese jumbo rolls circumvent the antidumping order on tissue paper from China.

changes.title: 2026 Section 301 duties on 60 economies reach every paper line
changes.detail: The 10% or 12.5% Section 301 duties on 60 economies (9903.05.20–9903.05.84) took effect. No Chapter 48 line is on the general exemption list (U.S. note 52(b)) or any country list, so they reach all 312 lines; only civil aircraft parts of 4823.90 are exempt (note 52(d)). Canadian and Mexican goods entered under USMCA are exempt (notes 52(g)–(h)).

changes.title: Antidumping order on crepe paper from China continued
changes.detail: After its fourth sunset review, the antidumping order on certain crepe paper products from China was continued for another five years.

changes.title: Section 122 surcharge expired
changes.detail: The 150-day 10% surcharge (9903.03.01) expired at the close of July 23, 2026.

changes.title: Brazil Section 301: 25% on all paper products
changes.detail: The 25% Section 301 duty on goods of Brazil (9903.05.01) took effect. No Chapter 48 line is on its exemption list (U.S. note 50(a)(ii)), so it reaches every line except civil aircraft parts of 4823.90 (note 50(a)(iv)).

changes.title: Paper plates finished in Cambodia and Malaysia: preliminary circumvention finding
changes.detail: Commerce preliminarily found that paper plates completed in Cambodia or Malaysia from paperboard made in China circumvent the 2025 antidumping and countervailing duty orders on paper plates from China, so such plates can be subject to the China orders.

changes.title: USMCA joint review: not renewed, still in force
changes.detail: The United States did not agree to renew the USMCA in its current form. USTR said the Agreement remains in force pending resolution of the issues or until termination, so USMCA claims (SPI S) still apply.

changes.title: Section 122 surcharge replaces the IEEPA tariffs
changes.detail: A 10% surcharge on products of all countries (9903.03.01) applied until July 23, 2026. No Chapter 48 line was on its product exemption list (9903.03.03); Canadian and Mexican goods entered under USMCA were exempt (9903.03.07, 9903.03.08), as were civil aircraft parts of 4823.90.

changes.title: All IEEPA tariffs end
changes.detail: After the Supreme Court held on February 20, 2026 (Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump) that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs, Executive Order 14389 ended the Canada, Mexico, China, Brazil and reciprocal duties, and CBP stopped collecting them for goods entered from 12:01 a.m. ET on February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Countervailing duty order on paper file folders from Cambodia
changes.detail: Commerce issued a countervailing duty order on paper file folders from Cambodia (4820.30.0040). Its antidumping investigation on Cambodia ended with a negative final determination.

changes.title: AD/CVD orders on thermoformed molded fiber products from China and Vietnam
changes.detail: Commerce issued antidumping and countervailing duty orders on thermoformed molded fiber products (molded pulp plates, bowls, clamshells, trays, lids and food or product packaging), listed under 4823.61, 4823.69, 4823.70 and 4823.90.10.

changes.title: Lightweight thermal paper orders on China continued
changes.detail: After its third sunset review, Commerce continued the antidumping and countervailing duty orders on lightweight thermal paper from China.

changes.title: Section 301 tariff on Nicaragua phases in from 2027
changes.detail: Products of Nicaragua that are not CAFTA-DR originating goods will pay +10% from January 1, 2027 and +15% from January 1, 2028 (9903.89.01, U.S. note 29), on every Chapter 48 line. The rate is 0% in 2026.

changes.title: Section 232 timber and lumber duties do not cover paper
changes.detail: Proclamation 10976 imposed Section 232 duties on softwood timber and lumber, upholstered wooden furniture and kitchen cabinets and vanities (U.S. note 37, 9903.76.xx). No Chapter 48 line is listed, so paper and paperboard pay no Section 232 duty.

changes.title: Antidumping order on paper file folders from Sri Lanka
changes.detail: Commerce issued an antidumping duty order on paper file folders from Sri Lanka (4820.30.0040), adding to the 2023 orders on China, India and Vietnam.

changes.title: Country-specific reciprocal rates take effect
changes.detail: Executive Order 14326 replaced the 10% baseline with country-specific reciprocal rates for many partners (for example 15% for the EU, all-inclusive). Paper products paid them until February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Brazil: 40% IEEPA duty on paper products
changes.detail: Executive Order 14323 added a 40% duty on products of Brazil (9903.01.77). Its exceptions did not include Chapter 48 goods other than civil aircraft parts, so Brazilian paper paid it on top of the reciprocal tariff. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Canada additional duty raised to 35%
changes.detail: Raised the IEEPA duty on non-USMCA Canadian goods, including paper and paperboard, from 25% to 35% (9903.01.10). Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: China IEEPA duties: reciprocal rate cut to 10%
changes.detail: Chinese paper paid IEEPA duties on top of Lists 3 and 4A: a fentanyl-related 10% from February 4, 2025 (20% from March 4, back to 10% from November 10, 2025) and a reciprocal duty that rose to 125% in April 2025 and was cut to 10% from May 14, 2025. All ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Reciprocal tariff covers paper products
changes.detail: 10% baseline (9903.01.25) on products of all countries except Canada and Mexico from April 5, 2025. Of Chapter 48, only exercise books (4820.20.00) are on the exemption list in U.S. note 2(v)(iii); all other paper paid it. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: AD/CVD orders on paper plates from China, Thailand and Vietnam
changes.detail: Commerce issued antidumping duty orders on certain paper plates from China, Thailand and Vietnam and countervailing duty orders on China and Vietnam (4823.61.0040, 4823.69.0040, 4823.70.0020).

changes.title: USMCA goods exempted from the Canada and Mexico duties
changes.detail: From March 7, 2025, goods entered under USMCA were exempt from the IEEPA duties on Canada and Mexico. Non-USMCA paper kept paying. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Additional duties on products of Canada and Mexico
changes.detail: +25% on goods of Canada (9903.01.10) and Mexico (9903.01.01), in force from March 4, 2025, including paper and paperboard. Ended February 24, 2026.

understandIndustry.why:
U.S. imports of Chapter 48 goods were **$19.94B in 2025**, down 3.9% from $20.75B in 2024 and below the 2022 peak of $22.40B. **Canada** is by far the largest supplier ($6.59B, 33%): uncoated printing and writing paper ($1.16B in 4802), boxes and bags ($972M), toilet paper, towels and tissues ($931M), fluting and recycled board ($826M) and kraft paper and linerboard ($555M). **China** ($1.92B) ships mainly toilet paper and tissues, boxes and bags, paper cups and plates and notebooks; **Mexico** ($1.70B) mainly boxes and bags; **Vietnam** ($1.04B) boxes and notebooks; **Finland**, **Germany**, **Sweden** and **South Korea** coated paper and board and specialty papers.

The biggest shift in 2025 was away from China: imports from China fell **37.5%** (by $1.15B), while Vietnam rose 22.6%, Indonesia 29.8%, and Malaysia and Thailand more than doubled, mostly in tissue, paper cups and plates and boxes. Several of these products are now under antidumping or countervailing duty orders on the new suppliers too (paper plates from Thailand and Vietnam, molded fiber from Vietnam, shopping bags from Malaysia and Vietnam), and Commerce preliminarily found in July 2026 that plates finished in Malaysia and Cambodia from Chinese board circumvent the China orders.

By product, packaging leads: boxes, cartons and bags (4819) were $3.56B, 18% of the total, followed by coated paper (4810, $2.35B), household tissue products (4818, $2.32B), uncoated printing paper (4802, $2.03B), plastic-coated and thermal paper (4811, $2.01B) and cups, plates and other articles (4823, $2.00B). 2025 is the latest full year of U.S. trade data, so the 2026 Section 301 and Section 338 duties are not yet visible in these figures. Duty-collected figures aren't available from an official source yet.

tariffEngineering.h1: HTS Chapter 48: Paper and Paperboard — Import Rules & Ways to Lower Duty

seo.title: Importing Paper & Paperboard: Rules, AD/CVD Scope and Legal Ways to Lower Duty (HTS Ch. 48) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: Tariff engineering for HTS Chapter 48: claim USMCA, classify to the right 8-digit line (the Canada Section 338 list turns on it), check AD/CVD scopes and circumvention findings, use drawback, and meet the marking, USMCA and FDA food-contact rules.

tariffEngineering.intro:
Every Chapter 48 line is **Free** under the general rate, so the levers are about the extra duties, and those turn on **origin**, the exact **8-digit line** and, for many products, the **scope of an AD/CVD order**.

For Canadian and Mexican goods, a USMCA claim removes the 10% Section 301 duty, but not the 50% Section 338 duty on 62 Canadian lines, and that list is drawn by 8-digit subheading: writing paper in rolls 4802.55.10 is listed and 4802.55.20–.40 are not, mechanical-pulp printing paper 4802.61.31 is not while 4802.61.10, .20 and .60 are. So correct classification, ideally confirmed by a binding ruling, matters. Next, check whether the product falls inside an antidumping or countervailing duty order; finishing it in a third country does not take it out. Then recover duties by drawback when goods are exported. Each rule and lever links to its regulation.

levers.title: Claim USMCA for Canadian and Mexican paper
levers.saves: 10% of value: the 2026 Section 301 duty on Canada (9903.05.29) or Mexico (9903.05.55), on every Chapter 48 line
levers.appliesTo: Originating goods of Canada and Mexico (all lines)
levers.document: A USMCA certification of origin from the importer, exporter or producer, in the importer's possession when the claim is made; it need not follow a prescribed format (19 CFR 182.12). Rules of origin: General Note 11.
levers.caveat: It does not remove the 50% Section 338 duty on the 62 listed Canadian lines (U.S. note 51(a)). The USMCA was not renewed at the July 1, 2026 joint review but remains in force.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. notes 51(a) and 52(g)–(h)
USTR statement on the USMCA joint review (July 1, 2026)

levers.title: Classify to the right 8-digit line: the Section 338 list and AD/CVD scopes follow it
levers.saves: 50% on Canadian goods when the product belongs in an unlisted subheading (e.g. 4802.55.20–.40 instead of 4802.55.10); the China List 4A rate (7.5%) instead of List 3 (25%) for 4814 and 4818.90
levers.document: Mill specifications showing the fiber furnish (chemical vs mechanical pulp, kraft share), basis weight, coating, brightness and ash, and the roll width or sheet size that chapter notes 5–8 and the subheading notes test. A binding ruling under 19 CFR part 177 settles the line before import.
levers.caveat: Classification follows what the paper is, not where the duty is lower. Note 7 sends paper that fits several of 4801–4811 to the last heading, and note 8 moves small cut sizes out of 4803–4809 into 4816–4823.

citations.label: HTSUS Chapter 48, notes 5–8 and subheading notes
HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. notes 20 and 51(b)

levers.title: Check AD/CVD scopes and circumvention findings before buying
levers.saves: The antidumping and countervailing cash deposits (company-specific; often far above the tariff) when the product is outside the scope
levers.appliesTo: Thermal and uncoated paper, sheet-fed coated paper, tissue and crepe paper, lined paper, gift boxes, shopping bags, file folders, paper plates and molded fiber products from the countries with orders
levers.document: The written scope in the order decides, not the HTS number. When unsure, ask Commerce for a scope ruling (19 CFR 351.225). Products finished in a third country from in-scope inputs can still be covered (19 CFR 351.226): Commerce preliminarily found that paper plates finished in Cambodia and Malaysia from Chinese board are, and is investigating tissue paper finished in Vietnam.
levers.caveat: Cash-deposit rates change with each administrative review; check the latest Federal Register notice and CBP's AD/CVD messages before importing. A supplier switch to a country with its own order does not help.

levers.title: Claim drawback when the paper, or goods made from it, is exported
levers.saves: Generally 99% of the eligible duties paid on paper that is re-exported or used to make exported goods (19 CFR 191.3, 191.51)
levers.appliesTo: All lines that paid an extra duty
levers.document: A drawback claim to CBP with the import and export records (19 CFR part 191).
levers.caveat: Antidumping and countervailing duties are not refundable as drawback (19 CFR 191.3(b)(3)). Check the Chapter 99 note and CBP guidance for whether a given extra duty is eligible.

levers.title: Enter paper gaskets and other aircraft parts of 4823.90 under the civil aircraft exemption
levers.saves: The 2026 Section 301 duty, Brazil's 25% and Canada's 50% Section 338 duty, for civil aircraft parts entered under General Note 6
levers.appliesTo: 4823.90.10–4823.90.86 (paper pulp and papier-mâché articles, paper gaskets, washers and seals, other paper articles)
levers.document: The General Note 6 civil aircraft certification on the entry, then the relief heading: 9903.05.88 (Section 301), 9903.05.05 (Brazil), 9903.03.16 (Canada).
levers.caveat: Only for parts for civil aircraft that meet General Note 6; the China List 3 duty is not lifted.

faqs.question: Are there tariffs on paper products?
searchedAs: are there tariffs on paper products
faqs.answer: The base (MFN) rate is Free on all 312 Chapter 48 lines, but extra duties depend on origin. Since July 24, 2026 the 60 economies in the 2026 Section 301 action pay 10% or 12.5% on every paper line (EU 10%, Japan and Korea 12.5%). Canadian and Mexican goods are Free with USMCA, except 62 Canadian lines that pay 50% under Section 338. China pays 37.5% and Brazil 37.5%. Countries outside these programs pay nothing extra. Antidumping or countervailing duties apply on top to many specific products.

faqs.question: Are there U.S. tariffs on paper from Canada?
searchedAs: are there tariffs on paper from canada
us tariffs on canadian paper products
faqs.answer: Mostly not, if the paper qualifies for USMCA: it is Free, and without a USMCA claim it pays 10% (9903.05.29). But since August 22, 2026, 62 Canadian lines pay a 50% Section 338 duty even with USMCA (60% without): unbleached kraftliner, greaseproof paper, some coated and thermal paper, writing paper in rolls and, since September 15, mechanical-pulp printing paper of 4802.61–4802.69, envelopes, napkins, corrugated boxes, small bags, notebooks, binders, labels and paper cups. Newsprint, copy paper, fluting, toilet paper and towels are not listed. The 2025 IEEPA duties (25%, then 35%) ended February 24, 2026.

faqs.question: Are there tariffs on toilet paper?
faqs.answer: Toilet paper (4818.10.00) is Free at base. From Canada or Mexico it is Free with a USMCA claim and 10% without; it is not on the Canada Section 338 list. From China it pays 37.5% (25% List 3 plus 12.5%), from Vietnam and Thailand 12.5%, from Indonesia, India and Malaysia 10%, and from the EU 10%. The antidumping order on "tissue paper products" from China covers lightweight wrapping tissue, not toilet paper.

faqs.question: Are there tariffs on paper towels and napkins?
searchedAs: are there tariffs on paper towels
faqs.answer: Paper towels (4818.20.00.20) follow the toilet paper rates: Free at base, Free with USMCA from Canada and Mexico, 10% or 12.5% from the 60 Section 301 economies and 37.5% from China. Table napkins and tablecloths (4818.30) differ for Canada: they are on the Section 338 list, so Canadian napkins pay 50% even with USMCA.

faqs.question: What are the tariffs on paper products from China?
searchedAs: tariffs on paper products from china
tariffs on paper goods from china
faqs.answer: Two Section 301 duties: 25% under List 3 (9903.88.03) on all paper lines except wallpaper and 4818.90, which pay 7.5% under List 4A, plus 12.5% under the 2026 action (9903.05.31): 37.5% or 20%. USTR confirmed on October 7, 2026 that the 2018–2019 duties continue. Many Chinese paper products also carry AD/CVD: thermal, uncoated and coated paper, tissue and crepe paper, lined paper, gift boxes, shopping bags, file folders, paper plates and molded fiber. The IEEPA duties on China ended February 24, 2026.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for toilet paper, tissues and paper towels?
faqs.answer: Heading 4818 when cut to size for household use: 4818.10 toilet paper, 4818.20 handkerchiefs, facial tissues and towels (U.S. suffix .20 towels), 4818.30 tablecloths and napkins, 4818.50 paper apparel and 4818.90 other (suffix .20 face masks). Large parent rolls of tissue, towel or napkin stock are 4803.00. Thin wrapping tissue in sheets is classified elsewhere, e.g. 4804.39.40.41 or 4811.90. All are Free at base.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for paper bags?
searchedAs: hs code for kraft paper bags
hs code for paper shopping bags
faqs.answer: Paper sacks and bags are in 4819: 4819.30 for bags with a base 40 cm wide or more and 4819.40 for other bags, including cones; U.S. suffix .20 is shipping sacks and multiwall bags and .40 is other bags such as grocery and shopping bags. Both are Free at base. Paper shopping bags (4819.30.0040, 4819.40.0040) from Cambodia, China, Colombia, India, Malaysia, Portugal, Taiwan, Türkiye and Vietnam carry antidumping duties, and Canadian bags of 4819.40 pay 50% under Section 338.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for corrugated and cardboard boxes?
faqs.answer: Boxes of corrugated paper or board are 4819.10.00 (suffix .20 sanitary food and beverage containers, .40 other); folding cartons of non-corrugated board are 4819.20.00; rigid boxes are 4819.50.40.40. All are Free at base. Canadian corrugated boxes pay 50% under Section 338 even with USMCA. AD/CVD petitions on corrugated pizza boxes from China, Malaysia and Türkiye were filed on September 9, 2026; folding gift boxes from China are under an antidumping order.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for paper cups and paper plates?
searchedAs: hs code for disposable paper cups
faqs.answer: Paper cups, plates, trays and dishes are 4823.69.00 (4823.61.00 if of bamboo): suffix .20 is cups and round nested food containers, .40 other such as plates. Molded pulp plates, bowls and cups are 4823.70.00.20. All are Free at base. Paper plates from China, Thailand and Vietnam and molded fiber products from China and Vietnam carry antidumping and countervailing duties, and Canadian goods of 4823.69 and 4823.70 pay 50% under Section 338.

faqs.question: What is HS code 4823.90?
faqs.answer: 4823 covers other paper and board cut to size or shape and other paper articles. 4823.90 is the catch-all: articles of paper pulp (4823.90.10), papier-mâché, punch cards, slide mounts, hand fans, paper gaskets and seals, cellulose wadding articles and other paper articles (4823.90.86, including paper shoe covers). All are Free at base; four 4823.90 lines are on the Canada Section 338 list, and parts for civil aircraft are exempt from the 2026 Section 301, Brazil and Section 338 duties.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for notebooks?
faqs.answer: Bound notebooks, diaries, address books, memo pads and letter pads are 4820.10.20 (sewn composition books are .30, other notebooks of 6–15 inch sides .40); exercise books are 4820.20.00 and binders 4820.30. All are Free at base. Lined paper products from China and India carry antidumping duties (and a CVD on India), and Canadian goods of 4820.10.20 and 4820.30 pay 50% under Section 338.

faqs.question: Are there antidumping duties on thermal paper?
faqs.answer: Yes. Antidumping orders from November 2021 cover thermal paper from Germany, Japan, South Korea and Spain (4811.90.8030, 4811.90.9030); the ITC began their five-year reviews on October 1, 2026. Lightweight thermal paper from China has had antidumping and countervailing duty orders since 2008, continued on January 23, 2026. Rates are company-specific and not included in the tariff calculator.

faqs.question: Are there tariffs on pulp, paper and newsprint from Canada?
searchedAs: us tariffs on pulp and paper
faqs.answer: Canadian newsprint (4801.00.01) is Free with a USMCA claim and 10% without; it is not on the Section 338 list. Most Canadian paper and board is treated the same way, except the 62 Section 338 lines at 50%. Wood pulp is a separate chapter (47) with its own exemptions. The Section 232 lumber duties do not cover paper or pulp.

faqs.question: Where does the U.S. import paper from?
searchedAs: how much paper does the us import
where does the us get its paper
faqs.answer: The U.S. imported $19.94B of Chapter 48 goods in 2025, down 3.9% from 2024. Canada supplied $6.59B (33%), then China $1.92B (down 37.5%), Mexico $1.70B, Vietnam $1.04B, Finland $990M, Germany $941M, Indonesia $744M, South Korea $665M, India $499M and Sweden $445M. Boxes, cartons and bags were the largest group ($3.56B).

faqs.question: What does HTS Chapter 48 cover?
faqs.answer: HTS Chapter 48, "Paper and paperboard; articles of paper pulp, of paper or of paperboard", is in Section X with pulp (Chapter 47) and printed matter (Chapter 49). It has 22 headings (4801–4823; 4815 is not used) and 312 ten-digit U.S. lines, all Free under the general rate: newsprint, printing and kraft paper, board, coated paper, tissue, wallpaper, envelopes, toilet paper, boxes and bags, notebooks, labels and paper cups and plates. Printed paper products whose printing is not incidental go to Chapter 49.
